Eighth grade science · Unit 8.1

Contact Forces & Collisions

Sixth grade (Unit 3: Forces, Motion and Energy) showed you that forces change motion. Now we get exact: how does a push turn into acceleration, why do two colliding objects push on each other equally, and how can engineers design cars so passengers survive crashes? Use Unit 0: How Science Works: we will predict, test, and compare.

Where we left off: in Unit 3 you learned that forces change motion and that energy transforms. You may already have learned that pushing something harder speeds it up. Now we get quantitative: how force, mass, and acceleration are connected, why forces come in pairs, and how engineers design for collisions.

Concept 1 · Newton's third law

Forces come in pairs

When object A pushes on object B, B pushes back on A with an equal and opposite force. The two forces act on different objects, so they do not cancel each other.

A force is a push or a pull, measured in newtons (N). Forces always come from an interaction between two things, so you never find a single force alone. Isaac Newton described this as his third law: if you push on something, it pushes on you. The two forces are the same size and point in opposite directions, but one acts on each object. That is why they are called a force pair and why they never cancel out: cancelling needs two forces on the same object.

Analogy

Pushing a wall on skates

If you push on a wall while wearing skates, you roll backward. The wall did not move, but it pushed on you with the same force you pushed on it.

Concept 2 · Net force and acceleration

How much a push changes motion

The net force on an object (all forces added, with direction) equals mass × acceleration. The same push gives a big acceleration to a light object and a small one to a heavy object.

An object's velocity is its speed and direction. Acceleration is how fast the velocity changes, in metres per second each second (m/s²). Often several forces act on one object at once, so we add them, with direction, to get the net force. If the net force is zero the motion does not change. If it is not zero, the object accelerates in the direction of the net force. Mass (in kilograms, kg) measures how much matter an object has and how strongly it resists changes in motion. One newton is the net force that gives a 1 kg object an acceleration of 1 m/s².

Analogy

Pushing a shopping cart

An empty cart speeds up quickly with a gentle push. A full cart takes a lot more push to get the same speed-up.

Try it

Data

Acceleration comparison

For a fixed force of 40 N: heavier objects accelerate less. This curve is called an inverse relationship.

Concept 3 · Momentum

What happens when objects collide

Momentum = mass × velocity. In a collision the total momentum before equals the total after (if no outside force acts). A heavy object that hits a light one changes the light one's motion more.

Momentum measures how hard it is to stop a moving object. It depends on both how much mass the object has and how fast it moves, so a slow truck and a fast baseball can have similar momentum. Momentum has a direction, the same as the velocity. In a collision (a short, strong interaction between two objects) the objects push on each other with equal and opposite forces for the same time, so one gains the momentum the other loses. Their total stays the same. This is called conservation of momentum, and it holds as long as no outside force, such as strong friction, interferes.

Analogy

Bowling ball vs. ping pong ball

A bowling ball hits a ping-pong ball: the ping-pong ball flies away fast and the bowling ball barely slows. Reverse them and the bowling ball barely notices.

Concept 4 · Contact forces

Friction and other contact forces

Friction opposes sliding; normal force pushes up from a surface; tension pulls along a rope; drag resists motion in air or water. All happen when objects touch.

A contact force acts only where two objects touch. Friction acts along the surfaces and pushes against sliding; rougher surfaces and harder pressing give more of it. The normal force pushes straight out from a surface, such as the floor holding you up (“normal” means at a right angle). Tension is the pull along a stretched rope or string. Drag is the push back from air or water as an object moves through it, and it grows with speed. A car's stopping distance depends strongly on friction between tires and road.

Analogy

Sneakers vs. socks

Socks on a wooden floor slide a long way. Sneakers on the same floor stop quickly. The surfaces grip differently.

Concept 5 · Engineering safety

Design a safer crash

A force is change in momentum ÷ time. If a crash takes longer (crumple zones, airbags, padding), the peak force is smaller. That is how engineers protect people.

Hitting something changes your momentum quickly, and the force you feel depends on how fast that change happens: force = change in momentum ÷ time. The same momentum change spread over a longer time needs a smaller force. Engineers use this when they design crumple zones (car front and rear parts built to collapse in a controlled way), airbags, seat belts and helmets. None of them remove the momentum; they make the stop last longer so the peak force on a person is smaller and less likely to cause injury.

Analogy

Catching an egg

Catch a raw egg by stopping your hand suddenly and it breaks. Move your hand back as you catch, taking more time, and it lives.

Check yourself

Can you explain it?

A 1,000 kg car crashes into a wall at 10 m/s. Explain why a car that crumples over 1 m is safer for passengers than a rigid car that stops in 0.1 m, using force and time.

Show a model answer

Both cars lose the same momentum, but the crumple zone stretches the stopping over a longer time and distance. Force = change in momentum ÷ time, so a longer time means a much smaller peak force on passengers (about 10× smaller here).

normal force

inertia

crumple zone
Part of a car that deforms to extend crash time.
Tutor notes: hands-on kit, misconceptions, pacing

Kit (about $10): two toy carts or rolling cans, a ramp, a meter stick, a stopwatch, a raw egg, tape, cotton, straws, a spring scale, books of different weights.

  • Concept 1: Roll carts down a ramp into each other with different masses; record speeds.
  • Concept 2: Pull a book with a spring scale across different surfaces.
  • Concept 3: Egg-drop challenge with a crumple-zone design and a budget.
  • Concept 4: Push a friend on a skateboard against a wall and note the reaction.
  • Concept 5: Graph force vs. acceleration for a cart with hanging masses.

Common misconceptions:

  • "A moving object needs a constant force." Only to overcome friction.
  • "The bigger object exerts a bigger force in a collision." Equal and opposite.
  • "Action and reaction cancel." They act on different objects.
  • "Heavy objects fall faster." Not without air drag.

Pacing: about five 30-minute sessions. Method link: run each lab as a fair test with one variable (Unit 0), predict first, then compare to the prediction.
